candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (an outcome patients value that the routine measure misses) and the neighbour viewpoint (someone who sees whether a person is lonely, not who is on the visitor list) led to contrasting what forms record with what the person feels; thermostat, house removals, stocktaking and small print were not used.
candidates.working_title: Living alone is recorded; loneliness is not asked
candidates.core_insight: Living alone, the number of visitors and feeling lonely are different things, and only asking the person finds the loneliness.
candidates.angle: Assessments treat household composition and visit frequency as a stand-in for loneliness, yet in a US cohort far more older people reported loneliness than lived alone, and in a large meta-analysis living alone was the weakest social measure for predicting death.
candidates.position: Loneliness should be assessed by asking the person, with a direct question or a short validated scale; 'lives alone' and 'daughter visits weekly' are not a loneliness assessment.
claims_needing_evidence: In a US cohort of 1,604 adults over 60 (Health and Retirement Study), 43% reported feeling lonely and 18% lived alone (cohort study; abstract read).
Because only 18% lived alone, most lonely participants must have lived with someone; confirm with the paper's own cross-tabulation before stating it (cohort study full text).
In a meta-analysis of 148 studies, living alone versus with others was the weakest measure of social relationships for predicting mortality (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.44) (meta-analysis abstract).
Objective isolation and subjective loneliness are distinct and behaved differently in adjusted mortality analyses in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (cohort study abstract).
A 3-item loneliness scale was developed and validated for use in large surveys of older adults (validation study).
evidence_leads: Perissinotto CM, Stijacic Cenzer I, Covinsky KE. Loneliness in older persons: a predictor of functional decline and death. Arch Intern Med 2012;172:1078-83. PMID 22710744 (abstract read this session).
Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Layton JB. Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review. PLoS Med 2010;7:e1000316. PMID 20668659 (abstract read this session).
Steptoe A et al. Social isolation, loneliness, and all-cause mortality in older men and women. PNAS 2013;110:5797-801. PMID 23530191 (abstract read this session).
Hughes ME et al. A short scale for measuring loneliness in large surveys. Res Aging 2004. PMID 18504506 (not yet read).
ONS 2018, guidance on the national indicators of loneliness (official web page; could not be opened from this environment).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In a US study of adults over 60, 43% reported feeling lonely, but only 18% lived alone.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: two labelled horizontal bars from Perissinotto 2012 (18 in 100 lived alone; 43 in 100 reported loneliness), no overlap drawn, and below them a question card with the three questions of the short loneliness scale. Credit line and series footer.
candidates.pause: A practitioner who writes 'lives alone, family visit' on every assessment sees two numbers that do not match.
candidates.gain: A reason to ask directly and three short questions to use.
candidates.follow: Shows the account turns measurement problems into a change the reader can make on the next assessment.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E010 (people living alone are less likely to get a dementia diagnosis) is about diagnosis; this is about how loneliness is assessed. No other overlap.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (ask what would change the decision), the front step, the son's viewpoint and the moment of discharge together gave a family question for the point when a ward says someone is not able to go home.
candidates.working_title: What would have to change for home to work?
candidates.core_insight: When a family is told a parent is not safe to go home from hospital, the useful response is to ask which specific problem makes it unsafe and what equipment, adaptation or support would change that.
candidates.angle: Turn a verdict into a list of problems that can be named and tested, and question permanent decisions made while the person is still acutely unwell; in Scotland most care home admissions come directly from hospital.
candidates.position: A permanent move into a care home should rest on named problems that home support could not solve, and should usually not be decided while the person is still acutely unwell in hospital.
claims_needing_evidence: In the Scottish Care Home Census 2012 to 2016, hospital was the most common source of care home admission (46%) (national descriptive study; abstract read).
In a linked Scottish cohort of people moving into care homes in 2013 to 2015, 57% moved in from hospital (cohort study; abstract read).
NHS England hospital discharge guidance advises that decisions about long-term care should not usually be made in an acute hospital bed (official guidance; exact wording to verify from a PDF copy).

Equipment and minor adaptations (grab rails, stair rails, key safes, raised toilet seats) can be arranged through occupational therapy or social care, and in England minor adaptations up to 1,000 pounds are provided free (legislation and official guidance).
NICE NG27 recommends involving the person and family in discharge planning and assessing the home where needed (NICE guideline).
evidence_leads: Burton JK et al. Who lives in Scotland's care homes? J R Coll Physicians Edinb 2019;49:12-22. PMID 30838985 (abstract read this session).
Ciminata G, Burton JK, Quinn TJ, Geue C. Understanding Pathways into Care-homes using Data (UnPiCD). BMC Health Serv Res 2024;24:281. PMID 38443919 (abstract read this session).
DHSC/NHS England. Hospital discharge and community support guidance (2022, updated 2024) (official; wording unsure).
Care and Support (Charging and Assessment of Resources) Regulations 2014 (England), minor aids and adaptations (legislation; unsure of regulation number).
NICE NG27 (2015). Transition between inpatient hospital settings and community or care home settings for adults with social care needs (official).
candidates.opening_line_draft: When a ward says your father is not safe to go home, ask which problem makes it unsafe.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card with four questions (Which task is unsafe? Is it the stairs, the front step, the bathroom or the nights? What equipment or adaptation would solve it? Can the decision wait until the illness has settled?) beside a drawn front doorstep with a new handrail. Series footer.
candidates.pause: A son or daughter who has just heard the words 'care home' for the first time.
candidates.gain: Four questions that turn a verdict into a plan that can be checked.
candidates.follow: Practical questions for families at the moments when decisions are made quickly.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E109 (getting home after hip fracture depends on thinking, standing, eating and toileting) is specific to hip fracture; this is about the home or care home decision and adaptations.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (follow the event over time) turned a cold spell into a timeline from hours to weeks; recipe card, container shipping, repairing and exceptions were not used for this candidate.
candidates.working_title: A cold spell's health effects last for weeks
candidates.core_insight: Deaths linked with cold weather stay raised for up to about three weeks after a cold day, more so in older people, so keeping warm is needed through the whole spell and the weeks after it.
candidates.angle: Follow one cold spell: blood pressure and blood thickness rise within hours of mild cooling in the laboratory, heart and stroke deaths follow within days, and breathing-related deaths continue for up to three weeks.
candidates.position: Older people should keep the room they sit in and their bedroom warm throughout a cold spell and for the weeks after it; the risk period is longer than the cold itself.
claims_needing_evidence: In 15 European cities (1990 to 2000), each 1 degree C fall in temperature was associated with a 1.35% rise in daily natural deaths, 1.72% for cardiovascular, 3.30% for respiratory and 1.25% for cerebrovascular deaths (multi-city time series; abstract read).
The cold effect was greater in older age groups and persisted up to 23 days, with no evidence of mortality displacement (same study).

Six hours of mild surface cooling raised blood viscosity by 21% and blood pressure, with little change in the first hour, in volunteers who appear to have been younger adults (laboratory study; confirm ages in full text before generalising).
WHO housing and health guidelines recommend indoor temperatures of at least 18 degrees C in cold seasons, and possibly higher for older people (WHO guideline).
UK cold weather advice for older people recommends heating the main living room and bedroom (official guidance; could not be opened).
evidence_leads: Analitis A et al. Effects of cold weather on mortality: results from 15 European cities within the PHEWE project. Am J Epidemiol 2008;168:1397-408. PMID 18952849 (abstract read this session).
Keatinge WR et al. Increases in platelet and red cell counts, blood viscosity, and arterial pressure during mild surface cooling. BMJ 1984;289:1405-8. PMID 6437575 (abstract read this session).

The Eurowinter Group. Cold exposure and winter mortality from ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, respiratory disease, and all causes in warm and cold regions of Europe. Lancet 1997;349:1341-6. PMID 9149695 (not yet read).
WHO Housing and Health Guidelines, 2018 (WHO; may be on NCBI Bookshelf; unsure).
UKHSA Cold-Health Alert and Keep Warm Keep Well guidance (official; not opened).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Deaths linked with a cold day stay raised for up to about three weeks afterwards, in data from 15 European cities.
candidates.visual_idea: Timeline diagram: cold day, then hours (laboratory study: blood pressure and blood thickness rise), then days (heart and stroke deaths), then up to about 3 weeks (breathing-related deaths), each labelled in words; a strip beneath lists practical steps (heat the room you sit in, warm the bedroom before bed, layers, hot food and drinks). Credit line.
candidates.pause: Older readers and families who think the risk is the one icy night.
candidates.gain: A time frame for staying warm and specific steps.
candidates.follow: Seasonal advice that is traced to evidence rather than repeated from a leaflet.

candidates.stimulus_use: The same operation (follow the event over time) applied to bereavement; the recipe card and the daughter's viewpoint suggested the everyday tasks the partner who died used to do.
candidates.working_title: The first six months after a partner dies
candidates.core_insight: The rise in risk of death after losing a spouse is largest in the first six months and clearer in men, so the surviving partner needs attention early, including the tasks the person who died used to do.
candidates.angle: The death of one partner removes, on the same day, the person who cooked, managed medicines, handled money, drove or booked appointments; the risk to the survivor is highest in the months when services have usually stepped back.
candidates.position: When a patient's spouse dies, the practice or team should contact the surviving partner within weeks and ask who now does the cooking, medicines, money and driving (a practical judgement; no trial has tested this).
claims_needing_evidence: In a meta-analysis of 15 prospective cohort studies (about 2.26 million people), the relative risk of death after widowhood was 1.41 in the first six months and 1.14 after six months (meta-analysis; abstract read).
The widowhood effect was clear in men (RR 1.23) but not clearly different from no effect in women (RR 1.04, CI 1.00 to 1.08), and did not differ between people under and over 65 (same meta-analysis).
The association is observational; proposed explanations include stress, loss of practical care and shared risks (review).
Widowhood is linked with changes in diet, particularly in men (cohort study; unsure).
No trial evidence was found for a structured check on the surviving partner (needs a search; state as an evidence gap if confirmed).
evidence_leads: Moon JR, Kondo N, Glymour MM, Subramanian SV. Widowhood and mortality: a meta-analysis. PLoS One 2011;6:e23465. PMID 21858130 (abstract read this session).
Stroebe M, Schut H, Stroebe W. Health outcomes of bereavement. Lancet 2007;370:1960-73. PMID 18068517 (not yet read).
Elwert F, Christakis NA. The effect of widowhood on mortality by the causes of death of both spouses. Am J Public Health 2008 (unsure).
Vinther JL et al. Marital transitions and changes in fruit and vegetable intake, EPIC-Norfolk, around 2016 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In pooled studies, the rise in risk of death after losing a husband or wife was largest in the first six months.
candidates.visual_idea: Timeline diagram across 12 months: first 6 months labelled 'higher risk (RR 1.41)', after 6 months 'RR 1.14', with a note that the effect was clearer in men; beside it a checklist card: 'Who now does the meals, medicines, money, driving, appointments?'. Credit line.
candidates.pause: GPs and community nurses who record a death but rarely think about the spouse.
candidates.gain: When to act and five things to ask.
candidates.follow: Teaching that fits primary care and community work, not only hospital medicine.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (name the trade-off openly) pointed to stopping driving, where safety and social connection pull in different directions; the other words gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Stopping driving: plan what replaces the car
candidates.core_insight: Stopping driving is linked with depressive symptoms, less social activity and poorer health, so the decision should come with a plan for how the person will get to shops, friends and appointments.
candidates.angle: Name both sides: stopping may be necessary for safety, and the loss of the car is linked with harm; the studies are observational, but the practical loss is real whatever the cause.
candidates.position: When an older person stops driving, for whatever reason, the plan should include transport to shops, friends and appointments; stopping without that plan is incomplete care.
claims_needing_evidence: A systematic review of 16 studies found driving cessation associated with declines in general health and in physical, social and cognitive function, and with greater risk of admission to long-term care and of death (systematic review; abstract read).
Pooled data from 5 studies: stopping driving was associated with higher odds of depressive symptoms (OR 1.91, CI 1.61 to 2.27) (same review).
The studies are observational and people often stop driving because their health is declining, so the association does not show cause (review discussion; full text).
Studies of 'driving retirement' planning or transport support after cessation are few (needs a search; unsure).
evidence_leads: Chihuri S et al. Driving cessation and health outcomes in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc 2016;64:332-41. PMID 26780879 (abstract read this session).
Marottoli RA et al. Driving cessation and increased depressive symptoms. J Am Geriatr Soc 1997 (unsure).
Edwards JD et al. Driving cessation and health trajectories in older adults. J Gerontol A 2009 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In pooled studies, older adults who stopped driving were more likely to develop symptoms of depression than those who kept driving.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card in two columns: 'What stopping is meant to prevent: crashes when driving is no longer safe' and 'What stopping is linked with: depressive symptoms, fewer social activities, earlier move to long-term care'; beneath, a question strip: 'How will you get to the shop, your friends, the GP, the hospital?'. Credit line.
candidates.pause: Families arguing about the car keys, and clinicians who advise stopping.
candidates.gain: A way to make the decision complete rather than only safe.
candidates.follow: Balanced decision posts that name both sides.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E016 (driving arguments force a dementia diagnosis into the open) is about diagnosis; this is about the consequences of stopping and planning transport.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (reverse the default assumption) and the quality 'averages' led to testing the assumption that loneliness is mainly a problem of old age, and to circumstances rather than age as the better guide.
candidates.working_title: Age is a poor guide to who is lonely
candidates.core_insight: In large surveys loneliness is reported less often with increasing age, and income, household, marital status, health and how often people socialise predict it at every age.
candidates.angle: Challenge the stereotype without dismissing lonely older people: target help by circumstances such as bereavement, poor health and living alone, and ask everyone.
candidates.position: Services should find lonely people by their circumstances and by asking, not by age.
claims_needing_evidence: In the BBC Loneliness Experiment (46,054 people aged 16 to 99, a self-selected online sample), loneliness decreased with age (survey study; abstract read).

In a nationally representative US sample aged 18 to 89 and over, loneliness varied with age in a non-linear way, and household income, household size, marital status, health and frequency of socialising predicted loneliness equally at all ages (survey study; abstract read).

ONS analysis of the Community Life Survey 2016 to 2017 found younger adults reported loneliness more often than older adults and identified widowed older homeowners living alone with long-term conditions as one higher-risk profile (official analysis; not opened).
Loneliness may rise again in the oldest age groups (needs source; unsure).
evidence_leads: Barreto M et al. Loneliness around the world: age, gender, and cultural differences in loneliness. Pers Individ Dif 2021;169:110066. PMID 33536694 (abstract read this session).
Hawkley LC et al. Loneliness from young adulthood to old age: explaining age differences in loneliness. Int J Behav Dev 2022;46:39-49. PMID 35001993 (abstract read this session).
ONS. Loneliness: what characteristics and circumstances are associated with feeling lonely? April 2018 (official; not opened).
Victor CR, Yang K. The prevalence of loneliness among adults: a case study of the United Kingdom. J Psychol 2012 (PMID 22303614 or 22574423; unsure which).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Many people think loneliness is mainly a problem of old age. In a survey of 46,000 people aged 16 to 99, loneliness fell with age.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: left 'Age alone' crossed through in grey with a text label; right 'Circumstances linked with loneliness at any age' listing only verified items (low income, living alone or small household, not married or widowed, poor health, socialising rarely). Credit line.
candidates.pause: Readers who assume every older person is lonely, and practitioners who target by age.
candidates.gain: A better way to decide whom to ask.
candidates.follow: Evidence posts that correct stereotypes about older people without false reassurance.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (examine a neglected consequence), with 'unpacking' and 'handovers', pointed to the partner left at home after a care home move, who is handed over to nobody.
candidates.working_title: The partner left at home
candidates.core_insight: When one partner moves into a care home, the partner at home often stays as distressed as before and has money questions of their own, so they need their own conversation.
candidates.angle: The care home plan is built around the resident; the spouse at home, who may visit daily and still help with care, becomes someone living alone with continuing strain and unfamiliar rules about the house and pension.
candidates.position: When a care home move is planned, the partner staying at home should be offered their own conversation about support and money, including the rules that protect the family home.
claims_needing_evidence: In a US prospective study of 1,222 carer and patient pairs, carers' depression and anxiety did not fall after their relative with dementia moved into long-term care, effects were most pronounced in spouses, and nearly half of spouses visited daily and still helped with physical care (cohort study; abstract read).
In England, the value of the home is disregarded in the care home means test while a spouse or partner still lives there (Care and Support Statutory Guidance, Annex B; official, not opened).
In Scotland, the home is similarly disregarded while occupied by a spouse or partner (Charging for Residential Accommodation Guidance; official, not opened).
In England, if a resident passes half of an occupational or personal pension to a spouse at home, that half is disregarded (official guidance; unsure).
evidence_leads: Schulz R et al. Long-term care placement of dementia patients and caregiver health and well-being. JAMA 2004;292:961-7. PMID 15328328 (abstract read this session).
DHSC. Care and Support Statutory Guidance, Annexes B and C (official; not opened).
Scottish Government. Charging for Residential Accommodation Guidance (CRAG) (official; not opened).
Age UK and Age Scotland factsheets on paying for care homes (charity; secondary).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In a US study, carers were as depressed and anxious after their relative with dementia moved into a care home as before. Spouses were most affected.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card titled 'When your partner moves into a care home, ask:' with three questions (Is our home counted in the fees assessment? Can part of the pension stay with me? Who will check how I am managing?), beside a drawn illustration of an older person at a kitchen table with letters, shown capable rather than helpless. Series footer.
candidates.pause: Husbands and wives at the point of a care home move, and their adult children.
candidates.gain: Evidence that their strain is expected, and three concrete questions.
candidates.follow: Posts that notice the people services forget to count.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (change the scale) and the timescale 'the last week of life' moved from dying in poverty as a population problem to the single form a clinician can complete for one person.
candidates.working_title: The terminal illness benefits form is a clinical task
candidates.core_insight: Fast-track disability benefit claims for terminally ill people depend on a short form from a doctor or nurse, and the criteria differ between Scotland and the rest of the UK.
candidates.angle: Many clinicians still think in terms of the old six-month rule or the DS1500; in England and Wales the threshold is now 12 months, and in Scotland it rests on clinical judgement with no fixed time limit.
candidates.position: Completing the fast-track form promptly, when the criteria are met, is part of good end-of-life care, and clinicians should know which rules apply where they work.
claims_needing_evidence: In England and Wales, the DWP Special Rules for End of Life apply when a clinician judges that a person may have 12 months or less to live, and the SR1 form supports the claim (official guidance; not opened).
The change from 6 to 12 months took effect for Universal Credit and ESA in April 2022 and for PIP, DLA and Attendance Allowance in April 2023 (official; dates unsure).

In Scotland, the BASRiS form rests on a registered practitioner's clinical judgement that the person has a progressive disease that can reasonably be expected to cause death, with no fixed time limit (Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018 and CMO guidance; official, not opened).
Under the special rules, Attendance Allowance or its Scottish equivalent is paid at the higher rate without the usual qualifying period (official).
Research for Marie Curie estimates that tens of thousands of people in the UK die in poverty each year (charity-commissioned report; figure unsure).
evidence_leads: DWP. Special Rules for End of Life: guidance for healthcare professionals on the SR1 form (official; not opened).
Scottish Government Chief Medical Officer. Guidance on terminal illness for disability assistance (BASRiS) (official; not opened).
Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018 (legislation).
Marie Curie with Loughborough University Centre for Research in Social Policy. Dying in Poverty, 2022 (report; unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In Scotland, a doctor or nurse can support a fast-track terminal illness benefit claim without predicting how many months the person has left.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card in two columns: 'England and Wales: SR1 form; life expectancy 12 months or less' and 'Scotland: BASRiS form; clinical judgement of progressive disease, no time limit'; footer line 'Check current rules where you work'. Series footer.
candidates.pause: Doctors and nurses who still think the rule is six months or the form is the DS1500.
candidates.gain: Current form names and criteria in one card.
candidates.follow: Teaching that covers the practical tasks around serious illness, not only the medicine.

candidates.stimulus_use: The thermostat and the operation (ask who bears the cost) led to the household paying to run medical equipment; the son's viewpoint and 'handing over' suggested a relative registering a parent.
candidates.working_title: Medical equipment runs on the household's electricity
candidates.core_insight: People who rely on powered equipment at home can join a free priority register with their energy supplier, and should ask whether any running costs are reimbursed.
candidates.angle: Equipment that keeps a person at home, such as an oxygen concentrator or a pressure-relieving air mattress, adds to the household's bills and depends on the power supply; two short calls reduce both risks.
candidates.position: Anyone using powered medical equipment at home should be on the Priority Services Register, and families should ask the prescribing service whether electricity costs are reimbursed.
claims_needing_evidence: Energy suppliers and network operators keep a free Priority Services Register; eligibility includes people of State Pension age, disabled people, people with long-term conditions and people who rely on medical equipment; it gives advance notice of planned power cuts and priority support (Ofgem; official, not opened).
The NHS home oxygen supplier reimburses the electricity used by a home oxygen concentrator (NHS home oxygen service; official; unsure for Scotland).
Some kidney units reimburse utility costs for home haemodialysis (NHS guidance or charity report; unsure).
Running costs of pressure-relieving mattresses, hoists and stairlifts are usually not reimbursed (needs a source; cut if none).
evidence_leads: Ofgem. Priority Services Register guidance (official; not opened).
NHS England Home Oxygen Service information for patients (official; unsure).
NHS England guidance on reimbursement of utility costs for home dialysis (2023?) (unsure).
Kidney Care UK reports on the costs of home dialysis (charity; unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: An oxygen concentrator, a pressure-relieving air mattress and a stairlift all run on the household's electricity.
candidates.visual_idea: Annotated scene: a drawn bedroom and hallway with labelled devices (oxygen concentrator, air mattress pump, stairlift) and a side checklist: 'Join the Priority Services Register (free)', 'Tell your supplier what equipment you use', 'Ask the oxygen or dialysis service about electricity refunds'. Series footer.
candidates.pause: Families of people on home oxygen or with an air mattress who have never thought about the bill or a power cut.
candidates.gain: Two phone calls with a clear purpose.
candidates.follow: Small practical details that other accounts skip.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (count something nobody counts), the stopwatch and 'distance' contrasted a timed walk in clinic with how far a person actually goes in daily life, which is what life-space measures.
candidates.working_title: Ask where they have been in the last four weeks
candidates.core_insight: Life-space assessment records how far, how often and with what help a person has moved beyond their bedroom, home, neighbourhood and town in the past four weeks, and lower scores are linked with higher mortality.
candidates.angle: Clinic tests time what a person can do in a corridor; life-space shows what they do, and it picks up the effects of transport, money and confidence as well as strength.
candidates.position: A mobility assessment of an older person should include a life-space question, because clinic performance tests measure capacity, not participation.
claims_needing_evidence: The UAB Life-Space Assessment documents where a person travelled during the 4 weeks before assessment, how often, and whether they needed help (validation study; abstract read).
In 998 community-dwelling adults aged 65 and over, physical function and performance explained about 45% of the variance in life-space scores and sociodemographic factors a further 13% (same study).
In 10,014 Japanese adults aged 65 and over, lower life-space scores were associated with higher mortality over a median 5.3 years, with an L-shaped relationship (cohort study; abstract read).
Life-space shrinks after disruptive life events such as the COVID-19 pandemic and job loss (cohort study; abstract read; optional).
evidence_leads: Peel C et al. Assessing mobility in older adults: the UAB Study of Aging Life-Space Assessment. Phys Ther 2005;85:1008-19. PMID 16180950 (abstract read this session).
Baker PS, Bodner EV, Allman RM. Measuring life-space mobility in community-dwelling older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc 2003 (unsure of pages).
Watanabe D et al. Dose-response relationship between life-space mobility and mortality in older Japanese adults. J Am Med Dir Assoc 2022;23:1869.e7-e18. PMID 35636462 (abstract read this session).
Lin SH et al. Life-space restriction following disruptive life events. J Gerontol B 2025. PMID 39807843 (abstract read this session).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Life-space assessment asks where a person has been in the last four weeks, from the next room to beyond their town.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram of concentric zones labelled bedroom, rest of home, outside the home, neighbourhood, town, beyond town, with small labels for 'how often' and 'help needed'; a caption strip: 'A shrinking life-space: ask about pain, confidence, transport, money, mood'. Credit line (Peel 2005).
candidates.pause: Physiotherapists, occupational therapists and geriatricians who rely on timed tests.
candidates.gain: A short, validated question set that adds participation to capacity.
candidates.follow: Clinical teaching that links function to the rest of a person's life.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E083 (strength fades when a parent starts sitting through the day) is about strength; this is about measuring how far people go.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (look at the smallest practical detail) with 'permission' and 'handing over' led to formal proxy access in place of a shared password.
candidates.working_title: Proxy access instead of a shared password
candidates.core_insight: A family member can be given their own proxy access to a person's online GP services, at a level the person chooses, instead of using the person's login.
candidates.angle: Older people who do not use the internet are often helped by relatives logging in as them; proxy access keeps the person in control of what is shared and leaves a clear record of who did what.
candidates.position: Families helping an older person with online GP services should ask for proxy access rather than share a password, and the person should choose what the proxy can see.
claims_needing_evidence: In England, GP practices can give a family member or carer proxy access to a patient's online services (repeat prescriptions, appointments, records) with the patient's consent (NHS England guidance; official, not opened).
Proxy access can be limited to certain functions, and the patient can withdraw consent (same guidance).
Where a person lacks capacity, proxy access may be granted in their best interests or to an attorney (same guidance).
NHS guidance advises people not to share their login details (official).
Adults aged 75 and over are the age group least likely to use the internet in the UK (Ofcom or ONS; official, not opened).
Arrangements in Scotland differ (needs checking; unsure).
evidence_leads: NHS England. GP online services: proxy access guidance (official; not opened).
RCGP guidance on proxy access to GP online services (unsure).
Ofcom. Adults' Media Use and Attitudes report, 2024 (official; not opened).
candidates.opening_line_draft: You can order your mother's repeat prescriptions online without using her password.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card: 'Ask the GP practice for proxy access: your parent agrees; they choose what you can see (prescriptions, appointments, records); you log in as yourself; they can change it at any time'. Drawn phone and paper prescription side by side. Series footer.
candidates.pause: Adult children who already log in as their parent.
candidates.gain: A safer arrangement that keeps the parent in charge.
candidates.follow: Practical fixes for everyday problems families meet.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E169 (medication apps fail when the person is unable to manage a phone) favours blister packs; this is about formal proxy access to GP online services.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (find the first question worth asking), the quality 'defaults' and the neighbour's viewpoint led to the next of kin box, which forms default to a spouse or child.
candidates.working_title: Who is in your next of kin box?
candidates.core_insight: The next of kin entry on a health record can be anyone you choose, including a friend or neighbour, but it gives them no legal power to make decisions for you; that needs a power of attorney.
candidates.angle: Forms that default to a spouse or children leave out people whose closest person is a friend, a neighbour or an unmarried partner, and families often believe the next of kin can decide for them.
candidates.position: Name the person you actually want contacted, and if you want someone to be able to make decisions for you, arrange a power of attorney while you are able to.
claims_needing_evidence: In UK healthcare, 'next of kin' has no legal definition for adults and gives no authority to make decisions (official guidance; not opened).
Anyone can be named as next of kin or main contact, including a friend (official or charity guidance).

In England and Wales, decisions for an adult who lacks capacity can be made by an attorney under a Lasting Power of Attorney or a court-appointed deputy; in Scotland by a welfare attorney or guardian (Mental Capacity Act 2005; Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000).
The Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act defines a 'nearest relative' who must be consulted in some circumstances (legislation; unsure).
Older lesbian, gay and bisexual people in Britain are more likely to live alone and less likely to have children (survey report; unsure).
evidence_leads: Mental Capacity Act 2005; Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 (legislation).
Office of the Public Guardian (England and Wales) and Office of the Public Guardian (Scotland) guidance on powers of attorney (official; not opened).
Guasp A. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people in later life. Stonewall, 2011 (report; unsure).
Age UK factsheet on next of kin (charity; unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: The next of kin box on a hospital form can hold the name of anyone you choose.
candidates.visual_idea: Drawn form section 'Next of kin / main contact' with several possible entries shown as roles (neighbour, friend, partner, niece); a side note: 'Being named here does not let someone make decisions for you. A power of attorney does.' Series footer.
candidates.pause: People without close family, unmarried partners, and relatives who assume the box gives them rights.
candidates.gain: A correction with a clear next step.
candidates.follow: Posts that give people without the standard family the same practical help.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (compare the stated aim of a service with what happens) and the home care worker's viewpoint led to comparing the legal wellbeing aims of care with visits commissioned by the minute and task.
candidates.working_title: Relationships are in the law; the visit has no time for them
candidates.core_insight: England's social care law names relationships and social wellbeing as part of what care should promote, while home care visits are often too short to include company.
candidates.angle: The gap is in how visits are commissioned, not in care workers' willingness; NICE advises against visits under 30 minutes except in specific circumstances.
candidates.position: Home care should be commissioned with time for conversation and connection counted as part of care; NICE's advice on visit length gives a standard to ask for.
claims_needing_evidence: Section 1 of the Care Act 2014 defines wellbeing to include 'domestic, family and personal relationships' and 'social and economic well-being' (legislation).

NICE NG21 recommends that home care visits shorter than 30 minutes are made only if the worker is known to the person, the visit is part of a wider package, and it allows specific tasks to be completed without rushing (NICE guideline; exact wording to verify).
Home care in England is commonly commissioned by time and task (needs a published source; unsure).
Scotland's Health and Social Care Standards include standards on supporting relationships (official; unsure of wording).
evidence_leads: Care Act 2014, section 1(2) (legislation).
NICE NG21. Home care: delivering personal care and practical support to older people living in their own homes, 2015 (official; may be on NCBI Bookshelf).
Scottish Government. Health and Social Care Standards, 2017 (official; not opened).
Homecare Association or The King's Fund reports on home care commissioning (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: England's Care Act lists 'domestic, family and personal relationships' as part of the wellbeing that care should promote.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: left 'What the law says care is for' (quoted wellbeing elements from section 1); right a clearly labelled 'Illustrative example' of a short visit timeline filled with tasks (medicines, meal, wash) and no time marked for conversation. Series footer.
candidates.pause: Care workers who know the problem, families who see it, and commissioners.
candidates.gain: The legal wording and the NICE standard to quote.
candidates.follow: Posts that examine the conditions that help or block good care without blaming the people who give it.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (ask who bears the cost), with 'queuing' and 'friction', led to unclaimed Pension Credit, where the cost of a complicated claim falls on the eligible person who never applies.
candidates.working_title: Pension Credit: why a small award is worth claiming
candidates.core_insight: Qualifying for Pension Credit, even for a small weekly amount, also makes a person eligible for other help, and many eligible households do not claim it.
candidates.angle: People decide the award is too small to bother with, not knowing that the linked help can be worth more than the award itself.
candidates.position: Anyone over State Pension age on a low income should have a benefits check, and practitioners who hear about money worries should point to one.
claims_needing_evidence: Pension Credit tops up weekly income for people over State Pension age on low incomes (DWP; official, not opened).

Receiving Pension Credit gives eligibility for other help, which may include Housing Benefit, Council Tax Reduction, a free TV licence at 75 and over, Cold Weather Payments, help with NHS dental and optical costs, and winter heating payments (official; check current rules, which changed in 2024 and 2025).
DWP estimates that a substantial share of eligible households do not claim Pension Credit [N to verify] (official statistics; not opened).
Claims can be backdated by up to 3 months (official).
evidence_leads: DWP. Pension Credit guidance (official; not opened).
DWP. Income-related benefits: estimates of take-up, latest financial year (official statistics; not opened).
Independent Age and Age UK benefits guides (charity; secondary).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Qualifying for Pension Credit, even for a small weekly amount, also makes you eligible for other help.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a central box 'Pension Credit' with lines to boxes naming only the linked help verified for the current year; footer 'Rules differ in Scotland; check where you live'. Series footer.
candidates.pause: Older people and families who decided the award was not worth the form.
candidates.gain: A reason to claim and a list of what it leads to.
candidates.follow: Attention to people on low incomes, with specific actions.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (test a familiar slogan against the evidence) was applied to the most repeated loneliness slogan; till receipt, cartography and auditing were not used.
candidates.working_title: Where the '15 cigarettes a day' line comes from
candidates.core_insight: The claim that loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day comes from comparing effect sizes across observational studies of social relationships; it overstates certainty, and loneliness deserves attention without it.
candidates.angle: Trace the slogan to a 2010 meta-analysis of social relationships of many kinds, show that a UK cohort found loneliness not independently linked with death after adjustment, and argue that the case for helping lonely people rests on their distress.
candidates.position: Loneliness should be taken seriously because it is distressing and linked with poorer health; the smoking comparison should be dropped because it compares unlike measures and implies a causal certainty the studies do not give.
claims_needing_evidence: A 2010 meta-analysis of 148 studies (308,849 participants) found stronger social relationships associated with a 50% increased likelihood of survival (OR 1.50); strongest for complex measures of social integration, weakest for living alone (meta-analysis; abstract read).
The 2010 paper compared its effect size in a figure with other risk factors, including smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes a day (full text; to verify in PMC2910600).
Most studies in the 2010 review measured social networks, support or integration rather than loneliness (full text; to verify).
A 2015 meta-analysis found loneliness associated with a 26% increased likelihood of mortality in adjusted studies (OR 1.26) (meta-analysis; abstract read).

In ELSA (6,500 people aged 52 and over), loneliness was not independently associated with mortality after adjustment for demographic factors and baseline health, while social isolation was (cohort study; abstract read).
The 2023 US Surgeon General's advisory repeated the smoking comparison (official; unsure).
evidence_leads: Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Layton JB. PLoS Med 2010;7:e1000316. PMID 20668659, PMC2910600 (abstract read this session; figure to check).
Holt-Lunstad J et al. Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: a meta-analytic review. Perspect Psychol Sci 2015;10:227-37. PMID 25910392 (abstract read this session).
Steptoe A et al. PNAS 2013;110:5797-801. PMID 23530191 (abstract read this session).
Office of the US Surgeon General. Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation, 2023 (official; unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: The line that loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day comes from a 2010 review of social relationships and survival.
candidates.visual_idea: Carousel, 3 slides: 1, the slogan in quotation marks labelled 'A popular claim'; 2, 'What the 2010 review measured': social networks, support, integration, living alone, with the plain-language finding and 'association, not cause'; 3, 'What a UK study found': isolation linked with death after adjustment, loneliness not independently, and 'Loneliness still deserves attention: it is distressing'. Credit lines.
candidates.pause: Anyone who has seen the slogan on a conference slide or charity poster.
candidates.gain: How to read a borrowed statistic, and a better reason to act.
candidates.follow: Careful evidence reading on topics where slogans travel faster than studies.

candidates.working_title: Phone calls that listen
candidates.core_insight: In a randomised trial, regular phone calls from briefly trained young callers who focused on listening reduced loneliness, depression and anxiety within four weeks in homebound adults.
candidates.angle: What made it work: an empathy-focused conversation led by the participant, the same caller each time, daily calls at first and then a frequency the person chose, delivered by lay callers rather than clinicians.
candidates.position: Regular phone contact from the same trained caller, led by what the person wants to talk about, is a practical loneliness intervention services can offer now; its long-term effects are unknown.
claims_needing_evidence: The trial randomised 240 Meals on Wheels clients in Central Texas in 2020; participants were aged 27 to 101, 63% were 65 or over, 56% lived alone and all had at least one chronic condition (RCT; abstract read).

Sixteen callers aged 17 to 23 were briefly trained in empathetic conversation; each called 6 to 9 participants, daily for the first 5 days, then at a frequency the participant chose but at least twice a week, for 4 weeks (same RCT).

Loneliness improved by 1.1 points on the 3-item UCLA scale (range 3 to 9); a second loneliness scale did not show a clear difference (P = 0.06); depression and anxiety improved; physical health did not change (same RCT).
Follow-up lasted 4 weeks, during the COVID-19 pandemic (same RCT).
Content of the caller training (for example, listening and letting the participant lead) to be confirmed from the full text (PMC7903319).
evidence_leads: Kahlon MK et al. Effect of layperson-delivered, empathy-focused program of telephone calls on loneliness, depression, and anxiety among adults during the COVID-19 pandemic. JAMA Psychiatry 2021;78:616-22. PMID 33620417, PMC7903319 (abstract read this session).
Masi CM et al. A meta-analysis of interventions to reduce loneliness. Pers Soc Psychol Rev 2011;15:219-66. PMID 20716644 (context; abstract read this session).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In a randomised trial, phone calls from briefly trained callers aged 17 to 23 reduced loneliness in homebound adults within four weeks.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram of the call schedule: week 1, daily calls for 5 days; weeks 2 to 4, the person chooses, at least twice a week; three labels beneath (same caller each time; the person leads the conversation; callers trained to listen), the last two only once confirmed in the full text. Credit line (Kahlon, JAMA Psychiatry, 2021).
candidates.pause: Befriending services, charities, practitioners and families looking for something that has been tested.
candidates.gain: A model with its active ingredients and its limits.
candidates.follow: Care that works posts that say what made the difference.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E165 (virtual visiting as orientation during delirium) is a different use of calls in hospital; this is a loneliness trial at home.

candidates.working_title: Welfare advice in the GP surgery
candidates.core_insight: Welfare rights advice offered in health settings consistently increases people's income, while evidence on health outcomes is weaker because the studies are small and of low quality.
candidates.angle: A care model with an honest reading: the financial gain is established; the health benefit is plausible but under-measured, which is an evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit.
candidates.position: Health services that see older people on low incomes should offer a route to welfare rights advice; the financial benefit is established, and better studies should measure the health effects.
claims_needing_evidence: A 2022 narrative systematic review identified 14 UK studies (2010 to 2020) of welfare advice co-located in health settings; all showed improved financial security for participants (systematic review; abstract read).
Some studies reported improved mental health; improvements in physical health were mostly subjective; overall scientific quality was poor (same review).
The review's modelled social return averaged 27 pounds per 1 pound invested (modelled estimate; state as modelled or omit).
An earlier systematic review found financial gains with limited evidence on health outcomes (systematic review; unsure of citation).
Some Scottish general practices serving deprived areas have embedded advice workers (grey literature; unsure).
evidence_leads: Reece S, Sheldon TA, Dickerson J, Pickett KE. A review of the effectiveness and experiences of welfare advice services co-located in health settings. Soc Sci Med 2022;296:114746. PMID 35123370 (abstract read this session).

Adams J et al. A systematic review of the health, social and financial impacts of welfare rights advice delivered in healthcare settings, 2006 (journal unsure; lookup in Health Soc Care Community failed).
Deep End GP project reports on embedded advice workers, Glasgow (grey literature; unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In all 14 UK studies of welfare advice offered in health settings, people came away with more money.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: 'Shown consistently: more income, debts addressed' against 'Not yet shown well: effects on physical health', with the number of studies and the quality rating stated. Credit line (Reece, Soc Sci Med, 2022).
candidates.pause: GPs, practice managers and hospital teams who meet money problems daily and refer nowhere.
candidates.gain: A service model with the strength and the limit of its evidence.
candidates.follow: Posts that treat poverty as a clinical problem with practical responses.

candidates.working_title: Attendance Allowance: four facts families get wrong
candidates.core_insight: Attendance Allowance is for people over State Pension age who need help or supervision because of illness or disability; income and savings do not count, you do not need a carer, and you choose how to spend it.
candidates.angle: Common beliefs (it is means-tested, you need a carer, it must be spent on care) stop eligible older people applying; Scotland has a replacement benefit with the same purpose.
candidates.position: Anyone over State Pension age who needs help with personal care or supervision should check whether they can claim.
claims_needing_evidence: Attendance Allowance is not means-tested: income and savings are not counted (DWP; official, not opened).
Eligibility depends on needing help or supervision with personal care because of illness or disability, whether or not anyone is providing that help (official).
There are two weekly rates [amounts to verify for the posting year] (official).
The need usually has to have existed for 6 months, except under the special rules for terminal illness (official).
In Scotland, Pension Age Disability Payment replaced Attendance Allowance for new claims [date to verify] (Social Security Scotland; official).
Receiving Attendance Allowance can increase entitlement to Pension Credit and other means-tested help (official).
evidence_leads: DWP. Attendance Allowance guidance (official; not opened).
Social Security Scotland. Pension Age Disability Payment (official; not opened).
Age UK and Independent Age factsheets on Attendance Allowance (charity; secondary).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Attendance Allowance does not depend on your income or your savings.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card 'Attendance Allowance: 4 facts' (not means-tested; you do not need a carer; you choose how to spend it; it is about needing help, not getting it), with a footer 'In Scotland: Pension Age Disability Payment'. Series footer.
candidates.pause: Older people and families who assumed their savings ruled them out.
candidates.gain: Four corrected facts and a reason to apply.
candidates.follow: Money information for older people that is exact and current.

candidates.working_title: Sexual health belongs in the history and the medicines review
candidates.core_insight: Many people in their 70s and 80s are sexually active, sexual problems are common, and most older people have not discussed sex with a doctor, so clinicians need to ask.
candidates.angle: A teaching point on history-taking: not asking is an ageist default that hides treatable problems and medicine side effects.
candidates.position: Clinicians should ask older patients about sexual health, particularly when starting or reviewing medicines known to affect sexual function.
claims_needing_evidence: In a US national probability sample of 3,005 adults aged 57 to 85, 26% of those aged 75 to 85 reported sexual activity in the previous year; about half of sexually active people reported at least one bothersome sexual problem (survey; abstract read).
In the same sample, 38% of men and 22% of women had discussed sex with a physician since age 50 (same survey).

In ELSA wave 6 (6,201 people aged 50 to over 90), a sizeable minority remained sexually active into their 80s; erectile difficulty was reported by 39% of sexually active men and arousal difficulty by 32% of sexually active women (survey; abstract read).
Commonly prescribed medicines such as SSRIs, some antihypertensives and antiandrogens are associated with sexual dysfunction (review or formulary; source needed).
evidence_leads: Lindau ST et al. A study of sexuality and health among older adults in the United States. N Engl J Med 2007;357:762-74. PMID 17715410 (abstract read this session).
Lee DM et al. Sexual health and well-being among older men and women in England: findings from ELSA. Arch Sex Behav 2016;45:133-44. PMID 25624001 (abstract read this session).
A review of drug-induced sexual dysfunction, or the BNF (source to find; unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In a US national survey of people aged 57 to 85, most had not discussed sex with a doctor since turning 50.
candidates.visual_idea: Two labelled bars from Lindau 2007 (men 38 in 100, women 22 in 100 had discussed sex with a doctor since 50) and a question prompt card: 'Has anything changed with sex or intimacy since you started this medicine?'. Credit line.
candidates.pause: Clinicians who have never asked a patient over 75 about sex.
candidates.gain: Data that make the question normal, and a form of words.
candidates.follow: Teaching that treats older people as whole people, including their relationships.

candidates.working_title: Winter deaths follow the house as well as the weather
candidates.core_insight: Countries with milder winters and poorly insulated housing had higher excess winter mortality, and among people aged 75 and over in Britain, winter risk was not confined to the poorer, so protection from indoor cold is needed for all older people.
candidates.angle: Two findings change how readers interpret winter deaths: indoor cold and housing standards count for more than outdoor climate, and in later life the excess reaches across income groups.
candidates.position: Advice and practical help to keep warm indoors should reach every older person, whatever their income, as well as those in fuel poverty (a judgement consistent with the authors' conclusions).
claims_needing_evidence: In 14 EU countries (1988 to 1997), Portugal had the highest excess winter mortality (28%), followed by Spain and Ireland (21%); higher excess was associated with milder winter climate and poorer thermal standards of housing (cross-country analysis; abstract read).
Colder northern countries such as Finland had lower excess winter mortality (same study; to verify in full text).

In people aged 75 and over from 106 British general practices, winter mortality was 31% higher than non-winter, with little evidence that the ratio varied by socioeconomic deprivation or financial worries; women and people with respiratory illness had higher winter ratios (cohort study; abstract read).
The Wilkinson authors concluded that fuel poverty policies may need to be supplemented by other measures (same study).
evidence_leads: Healy JD. Excess winter mortality in Europe: a cross country analysis identifying key risk factors. J Epidemiol Community Health 2003;57:784-9. PMID 14573581 (abstract read this session).
Wilkinson P et al. Vulnerability to winter mortality in elderly people in Britain: population based study. BMJ 2004;329:647. PMID 15315961 (abstract read this session).
The Eurowinter Group. Lancet 1997;349:1341-6. PMID 9149695 (not yet read).
Marmot Review Team. The Health Impacts of Cold Homes and Fuel Poverty, 2011 (report; unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Portugal, a country with mild winters, had the highest excess winter death rate of 14 EU countries in the 1990s.
candidates.visual_idea: Bar chart of excess winter mortality by country from Healy 2003, using only values verified from the full text, with the period and definition labelled; a second panel states the Wilkinson finding in plain words. Credit lines.
candidates.pause: Readers who assume cold weather deaths are a problem of cold countries or only of poor households.
candidates.gain: A different reading of winter deaths that points indoors.
candidates.follow: Evidence posts that change how a familiar problem is understood.

candidates.working_title: 'Social admission' is where assessment starts
candidates.core_insight: Older people labelled 'social admission' or 'failure to cope' often have an acute medical problem, and the label is linked with delays and missed diagnoses.
candidates.angle: A common shortcut that needs qualifying: a person who can no longer manage at home has a reason, and the label ends the search too early.
candidates.position: An older person who 'can't cope at home' has a problem that needs a diagnosis; a 'social admission' label should prompt a full medical and functional assessment, not replace it.
claims_needing_evidence: In a Vancouver matched study of 60 people aged 65 and over admitted with 'failure to thrive' or 'failure to cope', 88% had an acute medical diagnosis at discharge; admission and discharge diagnoses agreed in 12% of cases against 95% of controls (case-control study; abstract read).
The labelled group waited longer from triage to admission (10 h 40 min against 6 h 58 min) and stayed longer (18.3 against 10.2 days) (same study).

In a Dutch cohort of 130 older adults socially admitted after low-energy trauma, 30% had a missed diagnosis, which was independently associated with higher 180-day mortality (HR 3.06) (cohort study; abstract read).
A review reported underlying medical problems in about half of 'social' admissions (review; abstract read).
The terms 'acopia' and 'social admission' have been criticised as non-diagnoses that disadvantage older people (commentary).
evidence_leads: Tsui C, Kim K, Spencer M. The diagnosis 'failure to thrive' and its impact on the care of hospitalized older adults. BMC Geriatr 2020;20:62. PMID 32059639 (abstract read this session).

Goovaerts L et al. Missed diagnoses and adverse outcomes in older adults socially admitted to the hospital after low-energy trauma. J Am Med Dir Assoc 2026;27:106352. PMID 42468057 (abstract read this session).
Samaras N et al. Older patients in the emergency department: a review. Ann Emerg Med 2010;56:261-9. PMID 20619500 (abstract read this session).
Oliver D. 'Acopia' and 'social admission' are not diagnoses: why older people deserve better. J R Soc Med 2008;101:168-74. PMID 18387906.
Granger K, Ninan S, Stopford E. The patient presenting with 'acopia'. Acute Med 2013;12:173-7. PMID 24098878.
candidates.opening_line_draft: In one hospital study, 88% of older people admitted with the label 'failure to cope' left with an acute medical diagnosis.
candidates.visual_idea: Statement card with the 88% finding shown as an icon array of the actual sample (60 people, count to be confirmed from the full text) and three prompts beneath: 'What changed, and when? What is the new diagnosis? What would this person need to go home?'. Credit line.
candidates.pause: Doctors and nurses who have written or read 'social admission' this week.
candidates.gain: Recent data to challenge the label and three questions to replace it.
candidates.follow: Teaching that defends older people against diagnostic shortcuts.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E128 (treatable lookalikes behind decline blamed on frailty) is related; this targets the 'social admission' and 'failure to cope' labels with new data.
candidates.delirium_check: delirium is not the topic (missed diagnoses in these studies may include delirium; the post will not single it out)

candidates.working_title: 'Did not attend' is a finding
candidates.core_insight: Repeatedly missing appointments is more common in the oldest and the poorest and is linked with higher mortality, so it should prompt a question about why rather than a discharge letter.
candidates.angle: The record counts the absence, not the reason: transport, letters, hearing, memory, cost, or depending on someone else to bring them.
candidates.position: For older people, a missed appointment should trigger contact to find the reason before any discharge back to the GP.
claims_needing_evidence: In Scottish general practice data (550,083 patients, 2013 to 2016), after allowing for the number of appointments made, people over 90 (RRR 2.20) and people in the most deprived decile (RRR 2.27) were more likely to miss multiple appointments; practice factors also contributed (cohort study; abstract read; reference groups to confirm in full text).

In linked Scottish data, patients with more long-term conditions missed more appointments, and missing appointments was associated with higher all-cause mortality, especially in people with mental health conditions (cohort study; abstract read).
Missed appointments are a risk marker; the association does not show that missing appointments causes death (study conclusions).
'Was not brought' is used in safeguarding for children and for adults who depend on others to attend (guidance; unsure).
evidence_leads: Ellis DA et al. Demographic and practice factors predicting repeated non-attendance in primary care: a national retrospective cohort analysis. Lancet Public Health 2017;2:e551-9. PMID 29253440 (abstract read this session).
McQueenie R et al. Morbidity, mortality and missed appointments in healthcare: a national retrospective data linkage study. BMC Med 2019;17:2. PMID 30630493 (abstract read this session).
NHS safeguarding guidance on 'Was Not Brought' (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In Scottish GP data, people over 90 were among the most likely to miss repeated appointments, even after allowing for how many they booked.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card 'Before discharging for non-attendance, check:' (Did the letter arrive, and could they read it? Could they hear the phone? How would they get there? Who brings them? Could they afford the fare? Did they remember?). Credit line.
candidates.pause: Clinic staff and doctors who sign 'DNA, discharged to GP' letters.
candidates.gain: Evidence that non-attendance is a warning sign, and a checklist.
candidates.follow: Posts that look at what routine records leave out.

candidates.working_title: Offline in a digital-first health service
candidates.core_insight: People aged 75 and over are the least likely to use the internet, so every online route to care needs an offline route that works as well.
candidates.angle: The gap between a service's aim (easier access) and the experience of someone without the internet, good eyesight, steady hands or confidence with screens.
candidates.position: Services should measure how well people without the internet get through, not only how many use the online route; an offline route should be as quick and as good as the online one (a judgement based on fair access).
claims_needing_evidence: In UK surveys, adults aged 75 and over are the age group least likely to use the internet [N to verify] (Ofcom or ONS; official, not opened).
Internet non-users are more likely to be disabled and to have lower incomes (ONS; official, not opened).
NHS England's digital inclusion framework recognises that digital channels can widen health inequalities (official; unsure).
A peer-reviewed source on internet use in later life in England, for example from ELSA (to find; unsure).
evidence_leads: Ofcom. Adults' Media Use and Attitudes report, 2024 (official; not opened).
ONS. Exploring the UK's digital divide, 2019 (official; not opened).
NHS England. Inclusive digital healthcare: a framework for NHS action on digital inclusion, 2023 (official; unsure).
Matthews K, Nazroo J, Marshall A. Digital inclusion in later life: cohort changes in internet use over a ten-year period in England. Ageing Soc 2019 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: The people least likely to use the internet in the UK are those aged 75 and over.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram of two routes to the same appointment: an online path and a phone, letter or in-person path, each with its steps drawn; labels 'What is usually counted: online uptake' and 'What should also be counted: how long the offline route takes'. Series footer.
candidates.pause: Practice staff, managers and older readers who have tried to book by phone at 8am.
candidates.gain: A clear principle for judging access arrangements.
candidates.follow: Attention to people poorly served by changes made for convenience.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E169 (medication apps fail when the person is unable to use a phone) is about one tool; this is about access to services.

candidates.working_title: In a heatwave, check on the person who lives alone
candidates.core_insight: In past heatwaves, the older people most likely to die were those who lived alone, did not leave home each day, were confined to bed, or slept on a top floor, so a daily check and a cooler room are practical protection.
candidates.angle: The heat risk profile is also a loneliness profile: isolation and housing together, with social contact and access to transport protective.
candidates.position: During a heatwave, relatives and neighbours should check daily on older people who live alone or rarely go out, especially in top-floor flats (a judgement drawn from risk-factor studies; no trial has tested daily checks).
claims_needing_evidence: In the July 1995 Chicago heatwave (case-control study, 339 pairs), risk of heat-related death was higher for people who lived alone, did not leave home each day, lived on the top floor of a building, or were confined to bed; social contacts, working air conditioning and access to transport were protective (case-control study; abstract read).

In the August 2003 heatwave in France, among people aged 65 and over living at home, lack of mobility, lack of thermal insulation and sleeping on the top floor under the roof were associated with death; dressing lightly and cooling measures were protective (case-control study; abstract read).
UK heat-health guidance advises checking on older people who live alone during hot weather (official; not opened).
No trial has tested structured daily checks (search to confirm; state as an evidence gap).
evidence_leads: Semenza JC et al. Heat-related deaths during the July 1995 heat wave in Chicago. N Engl J Med 1996;335:84-90. PMID 8649494 (abstract read this session).
Vandentorren S et al. August 2003 heat wave in France: risk factors for death of elderly people living at home. Eur J Public Health 2006;16:583-91. PMID 17028103 (abstract read this session).
UKHSA Heat-Health Alert and Beat the Heat guidance (official; not opened).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In the 1995 Chicago heatwave, living alone and not leaving home each day were among the strongest risk factors for death.
candidates.visual_idea: Annotated scene: a drawn top-floor flat under the roof with an older resident, a fan, curtains drawn against the sun, water within reach, and a neighbour at the door; labels name the risk factors and protective factors from the two studies. Credit lines.
candidates.pause: Neighbours and relatives of older people who live alone, at the start of a hot spell.
candidates.gain: Who to check on, and what helps.
candidates.follow: Seasonal posts that link housing and isolation to health.

candidates.working_title: Ask who is important before you ask about marriage
candidates.core_insight: Assessment questions that assume a spouse or children miss the people who are closest to many older adults, including partners, friends and chosen family.
candidates.angle: A small change of wording in assessments helps the people most often left out, including lesbian, gay and bisexual older people, who are more likely to live alone and rely on services.
candidates.position: Assessments should ask 'Who is important to you?' and 'Who should we involve?' before assuming a spouse or children.
claims_needing_evidence: In a British survey, older lesbian, gay and bisexual people were more likely than heterosexual peers to be single and to live alone, and less likely to have children or to see family weekly (survey report; unsure).
Living arrangements are linked with loneliness in LGB older adults (peer-reviewed study; unsure).
Care Quality Commission guidance says adult social care services should support people's relationships and sexuality, including LGBT people (official guidance; unsure).
evidence_leads: Guasp A. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people in later life. Stonewall, 2011 (report; unsure).
Kim HJ, Fredriksen-Goldsen KI. Living arrangement and loneliness among lesbian, gay, and bisexual older adults. Gerontologist 2016 (unsure).
Care Quality Commission. Relationships and sexuality in adult social care services, 2019 (official; unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Ask 'Who is important to you?' before you ask 'Are you married?'
candidates.visual_idea: Question card showing two versions of one assessment question side by side, labelled 'Assumes' ('Are you married? Do you have children?') and 'Asks' ('Who is important to you? Who should we involve?'). Series footer.
candidates.pause: Staff who complete admission and care home assessment forms.
candidates.gain: Wording that finds the right people to involve.
candidates.follow: Posts that make services fit the people they serve.

candidates.working_title: Social prescribing for loneliness: an evidence gap
candidates.core_insight: Social prescribing is widely used for loneliness, but UK evaluations have mostly been small, uncontrolled and at high risk of bias, which is an evidence gap rather than proof that it does not work.
candidates.angle: Keep the distinction between absent evidence and negative evidence; among randomised loneliness interventions, the largest effects came from addressing how people think about social situations rather than from more contact alone.
candidates.position: Referral for loneliness should start with what the person wants and should be followed by asking whether they feel less lonely; services should be evaluated with comparison groups.
claims_needing_evidence: A 2017 systematic review of 15 UK evaluations of social prescribing rated all at high risk of bias; most presented positive conclusions despite design weaknesses; evidence was insufficient to judge success or value for money (systematic review; abstract read).

In a meta-analysis of loneliness interventions, randomised studies showed smaller effects than uncontrolled ones, and the most successful randomised interventions addressed maladaptive social cognition (meta-analysis; abstract read).
Reviews published since 2020 still describe limited high-quality evidence for social prescribing (systematic review; to find).
evidence_leads: Bickerdike L et al. Social prescribing: less rhetoric and more reality. A systematic review of the evidence. BMJ Open 2017;7:e013384. PMID 28389486 (abstract read this session).
Masi CM et al. A meta-analysis of interventions to reduce loneliness. Pers Soc Psychol Rev 2011;15:219-66. PMID 20716644 (abstract read this session).
Kiely B et al. Effect of social prescribing link workers on health outcomes and costs: a systematic review. BMJ Open 2022 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In a systematic review of 15 UK social prescribing evaluations, every one was rated at high risk of bias.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card teaching the distinction: 'Evidence gap: not enough good studies to know' against 'Evidence of no benefit: good studies that found no effect', with social prescribing for loneliness placed on the gap side and a note on what better studies would need. Credit line.
candidates.pause: GPs and link workers who refer for loneliness, and commissioners.
candidates.gain: An exact reading of the evidence and what to measure.
candidates.follow: Evidence posts that avoid both hype and dismissal.

candidates.working_title: Handrails on the front step: reading a home repair trial
candidates.core_insight: Low-cost home repairs (handrails, grab rails, outdoor lighting, non-slip surfaces) reduced injuries from falls at home in a New Zealand trial, but the headline figure depends on the analysis and the trial included people of all ages.
candidates.angle: Reconcile two results from one trial (the unadjusted comparison did not show a clear difference; the adjusted, exposure-based estimate was 26% lower) and state who was studied.
candidates.position: Simple home repairs are a reasonable, low-cost way to reduce injuries from falls at home; the trial supports them, with less certainty than the headline 26% suggests.
claims_needing_evidence: The HIPI cluster RCT included 842 households (1,848 occupants) in Taranaki, New Zealand, in owner-occupied homes built before 1980 with at least one member receiving state benefits (RCT; abstract read).
Modifications included handrails for outside steps and internal stairs, bathroom grab rails, outside lighting, edging for outside steps and slip-resistant surfacing outdoors (same RCT).

Crude rate of fall injuries 0.061 against 0.072 per person per year (relative rate 0.86, CI 0.66 to 1.12); adjusted rate per year exposed 26% lower (0.74, CI 0.58 to 0.94); injuries specific to the modifications 39% lower (same RCT).
Participants were of all ages, not only older people; the age breakdown and any older-age subgroup to be checked in the full text.
evidence_leads: Keall MD et al. Home modifications to reduce injuries from falls in the Home Injury Prevention Intervention (HIPI) study: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. Lancet 2015;385:231-8. PMID 25255696 (abstract read this session).
Clemson L et al. Environmental interventions for preventing falls in older people living in the community. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: A trial of cheap home repairs in New Zealand reported 26% fewer injuries from falls at home. The simpler, unadjusted comparison did not show a clear difference.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a drawn house cut-away with the six modifications labelled; a side panel explains the two results in plain words and names the trial population. Credit line (Keall, Lancet, 2015).
candidates.pause: Practitioners who quote the 26% figure, and those who dismiss home repairs.
candidates.gain: How to read a headline effect that depends on the analysis.
candidates.follow: Evidence reading that states the result that went the other way.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E068 (occupational therapy home-hazard work targeted at higher-risk people reduces falls) and E077 (feet, footwear, steps in the dark) are related; this reads one trial of builder-installed repairs in a low-income, all-age population and reconciles its two results.

candidates.working_title: New social withdrawal: risk factor or early sign?
candidates.core_insight: Less social contact is linked with later dementia, but withdrawal from friends can also reflect early cognitive change, low mood or hearing loss, so new withdrawal in later life needs assessment as well as encouragement.
candidates.angle: Reverse causation has a clinical use: advice to 'get out more' can miss the reason the person stopped going out.
candidates.position: When an older person newly withdraws from friends and activities, clinicians should ask about mood, hearing and memory before treating it only as a lifestyle risk.
claims_needing_evidence: The 2024 Lancet Commission lists social isolation among 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia (commission report).

In Whitehall II (28-year follow-up), more frequent social contact at age 60 was associated with lower dementia risk (HR 0.88 per SD), driven by contact with friends rather than relatives; the authors note that maintaining social contact may partly be a marker of cognitive reserve (cohort study; abstract read).
Studies with short follow-up are susceptible to reverse causation, in which early dementia reduces social contact (methodological point made in Sommerlad 2019; confirm wording).
Social withdrawal and apathy can be early features of neurodegenerative disease (diagnostic criteria paper; unsure).
evidence_leads: Livingston G et al. Dementia prevention, intervention, and care: 2024 report of the Lancet standing Commission. Lancet 2024. PMID 39096926 (not yet read).

Sommerlad A et al. Association of social contact with dementia and cognition: 28-year follow-up of the Whitehall II cohort study. PLoS Med 2019;16:e1002862. PMID 31374073 (abstract read this session).
Kuiper JS et al. Social relationships and risk of dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Ageing Res Rev 2015;22:39-57. PMID 25956016 (not yet read).
Ismail Z et al. Mild behavioral impairment provisional diagnostic criteria. Alzheimers Dement 2016 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Seeing friends less often is linked with later dementia, and in some people the withdrawal is an early sign of the illness itself.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram with two arrows between 'less social contact' and 'dementia': one labelled 'possible risk factor', the other 'possible early sign'; beneath, 'New withdrawal: ask about mood, hearing, memory'. Credit line.
candidates.pause: Clinicians who give prevention advice without asking why the person stopped going out.
candidates.gain: How to read a risk-factor list and what to do with new withdrawal.
candidates.follow: Teaching that reads prevention evidence carefully.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E005 (dementias that present as apathy or not coping) and E006 (check hearing before concluding dementia) touch this; the new point is how to read social isolation as a risk factor and what new withdrawal should prompt.
